end.summary:
Practised safe water storage: covered, clean containers and using a ladle or tap.
Discussed how dust, insects, mosquito eggs and germs can enter uncovered water.
Explored clear-looking water, filtering, boiling, dissolving and melting.
Practised ways to save water during brushing, bathing and watering plants.
Teach-back was not passed; dissolving and melting confusion was corrected later in the lesson.
end.parentNote: Pari practised keeping drinking water in clean, covered containers and taking it with a ladle, using reasons such as preventing dust and germs from entering. They explained that clear-looking water may still contain unseen germs or dissolved salt, and later corrected the mix-up by saying sugar dissolves while ice melts. At home, ask Pari to explain one safe-storage rule and one water-saving action using a real container or tap.

did.title: Storing and saving water

cards.ask: You found the clear water tasted salty. Why can't we always tell whether water is safe just by looking at it?
cards.answer: Dikhne se pata nahi chalta kyunki... salt toh paani mein dissolve ho gaya, dikha

cards.ask: If you taste a drop, will it taste like plain water or salty?
cards.answer: Salty! Salt gayab dikhta hai lekin taste toh namkeen hi hoga na, kyunki woh paan

cards.ask: Water from a tap has been kept in an open bucket for a week. Is it safe to drink?
cards.answer: No — dust, germs or mosquito eggs may ha

skills.skill: Store drinking water safely: clean, covered containers, a ladle or tap, regular cleaning
Know that clear-looking water can hide germs or dissolved things, and that dissolving is not the same as melting

misconceptions.belief: When sugar or salt dissolves it is gone — or it has 'melted' like ice.
